verses.15:
Al-Mizan presents this fifty-verse Meccan sūrah as a warning-centered affirmation of the Day of Separation, the Resurrection: its repeated ‘Woe to the deniers on that day!’—ten times—makes its threatening aspect more prominent than its good promise.

Al-Mizan reads the first six oaths as describing successive groups of angels of revelation, culminating in the near-explicit description of those who inspire remembrance in order to warn and complete God’s proof. Although the first two expressions in isolation apparently indicate consecutive cyclones and severe storms, it rejects both the reading that all five are winds, because the final three then require contrivance, and the division of the first two as winds and the rest as angels, because their common sequence lacks a clear connection. It also finds the proposed reference to prophets unsupported by what follows. Its reading accords with the analogous angelic oaths in (37:1-3) and the guarded communication of revelation in (72:26-28). A translator’s note nevertheless says that Chapters 51 (al-Dhāriyāt) and 79 (al-Nāziʿāt) similarly allow winds, clouds, ships, and related things to be correlated with the angels as intermediate directors of natural phenomena, leaving those identifications open and reconcilable.

Mursalāt derives from irsāl, dispatching or releasing, the opposite of imsāk; its feminine plural can refer to angelic jamāʿāt or to the Spirit (rūḥ) descending with angels, as in (16:2) and (40:15). Al-Mizan takes ʿurfan primarily as successive like a horse’s mane, so the oath is by angels sent one after another; it records the other sense, maʿrūf, in which it can mean dispatch for a good cause or for enjoining good. The fāʾ in (77:2) makes the tempestuous movement consequential on their dispatch: ʿaṣfi, rapid flow, figuratively describes the angels’ swift missions. Nashr in (77:3) is their unrolling the scrolls of revelation for the prophet, supported by (80:11-16), rather than winds spreading mercy or clouds—readings connected with (7:57), (25:48), and (27:63)—angels unrolling deeds’ records, or angels spreading their wings. Their farq then distinguishes truth from falsehood and lawful from unlawful; remembrance is either the Qur’an specifically or revelation generally. These are consecutive stages: opening the scrolls initiates that distinction and communicating remembrance brings it to completion.

Al-Mizan explains ʿudhran and nudhran as the purpose of inspiring remembrance. The conjunction may diversify the two ends: revelation completes God’s argument against deniers and warns others. It also records the reading in which the terms mean a means of excuse or exoneration for believers and warning for others. The consequent assertion (77:7) concerns all humankind: the promised Resurrection, reward, and punishment will certainly occur. Wāqiʿ is stronger than a mere statement of being because it conveys settled, firm occurrence.

The commentary calls the opening oath a Qur’anic rhetorical device that both emphasizes and proves its conclusion. God’s ordering of human affairs through revelation, moral differentiation, and warning is incomplete without obligation; obligation in turn requires a fixed meeting for recompense. Thus the sworn divine plan is itself the proof of retribution. It illustrates the pattern with sustenance grounded in the Lordship of heaven and earth (51:23), the Prophet’s protected purity contrasting with his people’s blindness (15:72), and the ordered cosmos and morally discerned soul supporting success through purification and failure through betrayal (91:1-10). Oaths such as (95:1-2) are more occult and require deeper contemplation.

Al-Mizan takes (77:8-11) as describing the promised Day by the end of the present cosmic order: stars lose their light and properties (ṭams; cf. (81:2)), the sky cleaves (farj; cf. (84:1)), mountains are uprooted and scattered (nasf; cf. (20:105)), and the messengers either receive an appointment to testify against their nations or reach the time for which they awaited testimony, as in (7:6) and (5:109). The same events recur in the smaller chapters: 78 (al-Nabaʾ), 79 (al-Nāziʿāt), 81 (al-Takwīr), 82 (al-Infiṭār), 84 (al-Inshiqāq), 89 (al-Fajr), 99 (al-Zilzāl), and 101 (al-Qāriʿah). Narrations call them ‘tokens of the Hour,’ a term drawn from (47:18). They mark the termination of a transient world, where life is mixed with death, gain with loss, joy with sorrow, action occurs without recompense, and apparent causes govern, before the categorically different eternal hereafter of uncompounded happiness or wretchedness, recompense without action. This contrast defines the new world by the destruction of the old and summons reflection on the first creation (56:62).

For (77:12), Al-Mizan prefers taʾjīl in its implication of deferral: the preceding cosmic events and the messengers’ appointment have been delayed for a day. It finds less apparent the alternatives that the pronoun concerns the messengers themselves or their news of the hereafter. The question-and-answer form—‘For what day?’ ‘For the Day of Judgment’—intensifies the threat and shock, as though inviting the hearer to ask what day could warrant such grave events. That Day is retribution and divine arbitration of disputes (22:17); (77:14) magnifies its significance. Wayl means halāk, destruction, and (77:15) curses the deniers of the promised Day. Because the apodosis of idhā in (77:8-11) is omitted, Al-Mizan understands either that promised punishment then befalls the deniers, or that this is the Day of Judgment on which they perish.

verses.50: Al-Mizan says these verses argue from God’s exclusive Lordship to the necessary Day of Judgment, where disputes receive their final settlement: deniers are punished, the Godwary rewarded, and the chapter closes by rebuking refusal to serve God or believe His word. Al-Mizan takes (77:16-18) as a rhetorical question affirming that God destroyed guilty ancient nations—such as the people of Noah, ʿĀd, and Thamūd—and continues to destroy later guilty nations. Itbāʿ means placing one thing after another. The second verse is an independent statement, not a continuation of the question: an authorial grammatical note observes that nutbiʿuhum would have been apocopated like nuhlik had it extended the question, and a translator’s note explains that the wording therefore states an ongoing divine custom, not only a past event. ‘That is how We deal with the guilty’ explains why they were destroyed. The commentary identifies three functions in this warning. First, it accords with the chapter’s repeated threat in (77:19). Second, it proves exclusive Lordship: destroying the guilty is management of human affairs, the polytheists acknowledge God alone as the destroyer, and therefore He alone is humanity’s Lord and the One to worship. Third, it proves Judgment: destruction for sin presupposes prior obligations, which are pointless without reward for obedience and punishment for disobedience. Since this world cannot contain every recompense, all must be paid for their deeds on the Day of Judgment, ‘the Day of Judgment’ (37:21), when all humankind is gathered (11:103). Al-Mizan similarly reads (77:20-23) as a rhetorical reminder that people were made from māʾ mahīn, an insignificant fluid, namely nuṭfah, preserved in the womb until the known term of pregnancy. Qadr is primarily the transitive taqdīr: after creating, God ordains the person’s future events, properties, and states—life-span, stature, beauty, health, illness, and provision. It records but finds less plausible the derivation from qudrah, which would mean only divine ability. This measured nurturing again establishes God’s Lordship, the servant’s humility and obedience, and hence the retribution that obligation requires. For (77:25-28), the earth is kifāt, either a gathering that accommodates living and dead alike or receptacles that contain them. Its lofty shāmikhāt and firm rawāsī are followed by sweet, potable furāt water because streams and springs descend from mountains to plains. Al-Mizan says the same proof of Lordship and Judgment can be drawn from these provisions. The guilty are then told by God—identified from (77:39)—to go immediately from the Resurrection plain to the hell they denied; inṭilāq denotes direct, immediate movement. The triple-forked ‘shadow’ is, according to exegetes, the immense plume of hell’s smoke, comparable to the dense black smoke in (56:43), branching with its breadth. It does not give the protective shade meant by ẓalīl and cannot shield from lahab, the upper flame. The fire’s sparks, sharar, leap out huge as palaces and bright like yellow male camels. Al-Mizan reconciles the silence and absence of excuses in (77:35-37) with verses that say people speak on Resurrection: the Day has stages, including stages of questioning and answering, and others in which mouths are sealed and no apology is permitted, as discussed under (11:105). The Day is al-faṣl because God decisively separates truth’s followers from falsehood’s through judgment, as in (32:25), (10:93), and (45:17). The address gathers the disbelievers among the Prophet’s people with the ancients, consistent with (11:103) and (18:47), then humiliates them: if they can devise any stratagem to counter God’s punishment, let them try. It manifests that all power belongs to God alone (2:165-166). This challenge is broader than the specifically escapist challenge in (55:33); the switch from ‘We’ to ‘Me’ heightens the point, since the humiliating command comes from the sole source of might. The Godwary, by contrast, rest in Paradise’s shade and drink from its springs, with desired fruit. ‘Eat and drink’ grants free permission, and apparently represents every kind of heavenly enjoyment, not food alone; (77:41-45) confirms their felicitous end. ‘Eat and enjoy a little’ to the guilty is instead a despairing rebuke: they may pursue transient worldly gratification, but it cannot avert punishment for denying the Day. It echoes (20:72) and (41:40), and their cattle-like conception of happiness is answered by (47:12). Al-Mizan takes ‘Bow down’ in (77:48) most apparently as prayer, because bowing is one of its elements. It reports two less apparent alternatives: general humility and devotion through accepting the message and worship, or Resurrection prostration as in (68:42). The refusal to worship accords with denial of recompense and prepares the final question. A connection attributed to al-Zamakhsharī makes this an added category alongside the deniers in (77:47). The shift from addressing them directly to speaking of them leaves them to the course they chose after ‘Eat and enjoy’ (77:46). Finally, Al-Mizan calls the Qur’an a divine sign and miracle that has expressed God’s exclusive worthiness of worship and the coming Day in the most eloquent discourse. If they will not believe that, no further discourse offers hope of their belief in God, His Messenger, or the Last Day. Their abandonment after ‘Eat and enjoy’ is therefore justified: continued calling brings them no benefit except the completion of God’s argument, leaving them no excuse.
